title: AI in the Workplace: What Changes When AI Becomes a Coworker?
description: A 75-minute facilitated lab on how AI is changing workplace tasks, workflows, skills, judgment, and human responsibility. Students move from individual judgment to team job redesign and an individual exit reflection.

steps.label: 🗳️ COLD OPEN
steps.title: Which workplace decision would you be LEAST willing to delegate completely to AI?
steps.lead: Make the call before we discuss it. The question is not whether AI can help. The question is where you would refuse to give it final authority.
choices: 📄 Screen 500 résumés and recommend the top 20
📝 Summarize a meeting and assign action items
🏆 Decide which employee receives a promotion
steps.studentTask: Vote independently. Then be ready to explain what changes as the stakes increase.
steps.roomInstruction: VOTE FIRST · THEN DEFEND YOUR CHOICE
steps.visualCaption: Where should AI help—and where should humans keep authority?

runbook.say: Before we talk about AI and jobs, I want your instincts. Which of these would you be least willing to hand completely to AI? Don't overthink it—vote first.
runbook.askNext: What changed between the customer email and the promotion decision?
runbook.watchFor: Consequence, fairness, personal context, sensitive data, reversibility, accountability, and the difference between AI assistance and AI authority.
runbook.advanceWhen: Most students have voted and you have heard 2–3 different reasons.
runbook.openWith: No discussion yet. Make your own call.
runbook.whyMatters: Surfaces students' existing standards for acceptable automation before introducing a framework.
runbook.ask: What changed between the lower-stakes and higher-stakes tasks?
runbook.pause: 30 seconds to vote; 3–4 minutes to hear contrasting explanations.
runbook.listenFor: Consequence, fairness, context, accountability, human judgment.
runbook.ifTheySay: AI should never decide anything → ask whether recommendation, ranking, or drafting can still be useful without final authority.
runbook.ifQuiet: Ask: Which mistake would be easiest to reverse? Which could change someone's life?
runbook.pushFurther: Does AI being accurate most of the time automatically give it decision authority?
runbook.sayDuringReveal: Notice that this is not really a yes/no question about AI. Your standard changes with the consequence.
runbook.landHere: AI assistance and AI authority are not the same thing.
runbook.transition: Now let's look at what is actually changing in work.

steps.label: 🌎 HAPPENING NOW
steps.title: AI is changing work—mostly by changing tasks first.
steps.lead: The useful question is not simply “Will AI take jobs?” It is “Which tasks move to AI, which become human + AI, and which require stronger human judgment?”
steps.studentTask: Listen for one change that could affect an entry-level role you may want.
steps.visualCaption: Work is being redesigned before entire occupations disappear.

runbook.say: AI is increasingly moving from answering questions to doing parts of workflows—drafting, summarizing, analyzing, recommending, coding, and now taking actions through agents. That means the workplace question is becoming: what do we delegate, what do we verify, and what must a human still own?
runbook.askNext: If everyone entering your field can use AI, what makes one employee more valuable than another?
runbook.watchFor: Students naming domain knowledge, communication, judgment, verification, creativity, problem framing, relationship skills, adaptability, and accountability.
runbook.advanceWhen: Students can name at least three human capabilities that become more important when AI is widely available.
runbook.openWith: Let's replace the headline 'AI is taking jobs' with a more useful question.
runbook.whyMatters: Gives students a current labor-market frame without turning the class into a news lecture.
runbook.ask: What becomes more valuable when AI can perform more routine cognitive tasks?
runbook.pause: Keep this mini-lesson to about eight minutes.
runbook.listenFor: Judgment, context, expertise, communication, verification, adaptability.
runbook.ifTheySay: Prompting → affirm it, then ask what happens when prompting becomes a baseline skill everyone has.
runbook.ifQuiet: Ask what a manager would pay more for: someone who gets an AI answer or someone who knows whether that answer should be used.
runbook.pushFurther: What happens to entry-level learning if AI performs the tasks people used to learn from?
runbook.landHere: Your advantage is not merely using AI. It is knowing what to delegate, how to judge the output, and when to take control.
runbook.transition: Now audit a job you may actually want.
runbook.sourceNotes: Reuters, Oct. 7, 2026: AI at Work discussion with ADP chief economist—AI is reshaping tasks more than eliminating entire occupations. LinkedIn Labor Market Report 2026: U.S. jobs requiring AI-literacy skills grew 70% year over year. WEF, Sept. 2026: employers increasingly value learning agility and distinctly human skills for young workers.

steps.label: 🧭 SOLO JOB AUDIT
steps.title: Audit a job you might actually want.
steps.lead: Choose a realistic role you could pursue in the next 3–5 years. Break it into tasks instead of treating the job as one thing.
steps.studentTask: Choose a future job. Identify one task AI could mostly do, one task human + AI should do together, and one task a human should remain primarily responsible for. Submit the human-led task and why.
steps.roomInstruction: AI DOES · HUMAN + AI · HUMAN OWNS
steps.visualCaption: Do not protect a task just because 'that is how the job has always been done.'

runbook.say: Pick a job you could realistically see yourself doing. Don't ask whether AI changes the job. Assume it does. Your job is to decide where.
runbook.askNext: Which task are you keeping human-led—and what is the strongest reason?
runbook.watchFor: Students protecting routine tasks without explaining human value; vague jobs instead of specific tasks; 'AI can't do it' claims that are really preference statements.
runbook.advanceWhen: Most students have identified all three categories and submitted one defensible human-led task.
runbook.openWith: This is individual first. I want your thinking before you hear anyone else's.
runbook.whyMatters: Makes workplace AI personally relevant and shifts analysis from occupations to tasks.
runbook.ask: What could go wrong if AI handled too much of this task?
runbook.pause: About 9 minutes individual work, then 3 minutes to capture submissions and sample responses.
runbook.listenFor: Human context, consequence, empathy, exception handling, accountability, domain expertise, safety.
runbook.ifTheySay: AI could do the whole job → ask who defines success, handles exceptions, and owns the consequences.
runbook.ifQuiet: Offer examples: cybersecurity analyst, developer, data analyst, marketing specialist, project manager, healthcare administrator.
runbook.pushFurther: Are you protecting this task because humans add value—or because this is how the job works today?
runbook.sayDuringReveal: Different jobs change differently, but the pattern is similar: tasks get redistributed.
runbook.landHere: Jobs are bundles of tasks. AI changes the bundle before it necessarily replaces the role.
runbook.transition: Now find someone whose judgment differs from yours.

steps.label: 🤝 PAIR COMPARE
steps.title: Find one task you disagree about.
steps.lead: Compare your job audit with someone near you—preferably someone considering a different field.
steps.studentTask: Compare your three categories. Find ONE task where you disagree about how much AI should do. Each person gets one minute to defend the choice.
steps.visualCaption: Useful disagreement reveals the assumptions behind your automation choices.

runbook.say: Your goal is not agreement. Find one place where your line between AI and human responsibility is different.
runbook.askNext: What assumption caused the disagreement—risk, trust, expertise, efficiency, fairness, or something else?
runbook.watchFor: Pairs agreeing too quickly; encourage them to test one another's reasoning rather than simply share answers.
runbook.advanceWhen: Pairs can name one genuine disagreement and the assumption underneath it.
runbook.whyMatters: Makes implicit standards visible before students redesign a role as a team.
runbook.ask: What makes one of you comfortable delegating more than the other?
runbook.listenFor: Different definitions of acceptable risk, human value, and accountability.
runbook.ifQuiet: Ask them to choose the highest-stakes task from either person's audit.
runbook.landHere: The boundary between human and AI work is a design decision—not an automatic fact.
runbook.transition: Now you get to redesign an entire role.

steps.label: 🛠️ TEAM CHALLENGE
steps.title: Redesign the job for 2028.
steps.lead: Your organization has powerful AI tools and agents. Redesign one role to get real value from AI without creating irresponsible automation.
steps.studentTask: Teams of 3–5: choose one role. Build three columns—AI DOES / HUMAN DOES / HUMAN CHECKS. Decide one task that shrinks or disappears, one human skill that becomes more valuable, and ONE thing you will not fully automate. One team member submits your non-automate decision + safeguard.
steps.roomInstruction: AI DOES · HUMAN DOES · HUMAN CHECKS
steps.visualCaption: Maximum value from AI ≠ maximum automation.

runbook.say: It is 2028. AI is not optional at this organization. Your team has to redesign the role responsibly—not preserve the old job and not automate everything.
runbook.askNext: What is the one thing your team refuses to fully automate, and why?
runbook.watchFor: Teams defaulting to 'AI does everything, human checks.' Push them to specify what checking means and whether the human has real override authority.
runbook.advanceWhen: Each team has the three-column design, one task change, one newly valuable human skill, one non-automate choice, and a safeguard.
runbook.openWith: Build the future job, not a list of AI tools.
runbook.whyMatters: Integrates task redesign, human judgment, risk, and responsible automation in one authentic workplace problem.
runbook.ask: Where exactly does the human have authority to stop, correct, or override the system?
runbook.pause: Give teams about 14 minutes to build and 4 minutes to finalize a concise submission/pitch.
runbook.listenFor: Clear task allocation, meaningful human review, exception handling, stakes, data/privacy, fairness, accountability.
runbook.ifTheySay: A human checks it → ask what they check, what evidence they need, and whether they can actually override the AI.
runbook.ifQuiet: Assign a role to each table.
runbook.pushFurther: Which part of this redesigned job would an employer pay a strong human performer more to do well?
runbook.landHere: Responsible job redesign optimizes the partnership, not the amount of automation.
runbook.transition: Now defend your design against the room.

steps.label: 🎤 DEFEND THE DESIGN
steps.title: Pitch it. Then let the room attack the weak spot.
steps.lead: Each team gets about 60–90 seconds: AI handles ____. Humans remain responsible for ____ because ____.
steps.studentTask: Choose a spokesperson. Give the redesign pitch. After each pitch, another student identifies one thing that could go wrong; the team answers with a safeguard.
steps.roomInstruction: PITCH → WHAT COULD GO WRONG? → SAFEGUARD
steps.visualCaption: A strong design survives a challenge.

runbook.say: You get one minute to convince us your redesign creates value without quietly handing away human responsibility.
runbook.askNext: Class: what could go wrong? Team: what safeguard would you add?
runbook.watchFor: Generic safeguards such as 'monitor it.' Push for a concrete review, threshold, appeal, audit, permission boundary, or override.
runbook.advanceWhen: Several teams have pitched and every pitch has been challenged with at least one risk/safeguard exchange.
runbook.openWith: Keep the pitches fast. The challenge is where the learning happens.
runbook.whyMatters: Requires teams to defend assumptions rather than merely report their work.
runbook.ask: What is the weakest point in this human + AI workflow?
runbook.pause: 60–90 seconds per selected team plus one rapid challenge.
runbook.listenFor: Specific safeguards tied to the actual risk.
runbook.ifTheySay: We would monitor it → ask what would trigger intervention.
runbook.ifQuiet: You provide the challenge: What happens when the AI is confidently wrong?
runbook.pushFurther: Who is accountable if the safeguard fails?
runbook.landHere: Human oversight only matters when it is specific, informed, and able to change the outcome.
runbook.transition: So what makes a person valuable in an AI-rich workplace?

steps.label: 🧠 VALUE SHIFT
steps.title: If everyone has AI, what makes someone valuable?
steps.lead: Choose the TWO capabilities you think will matter most in your future work.
choices: 🧩 Problem framing + asking the right questions
steps.studentTask: Choose exactly TWO. Then compare the class results with what employers actually need from people working with AI.
steps.roomInstruction: CHOOSE TWO · WHAT BECOMES MORE VALUABLE?
steps.visualCaption: AI literacy is becoming baseline. Human value moves up the stack.

runbook.say: If AI access becomes ordinary, 'I know how to use AI' stops being much of a differentiator. So what moves up in value?
runbook.askNext: Why did you choose those two—and which one is hardest to automate?
runbook.watchFor: Students choosing only technical skills. Use the results to connect technical capability with judgment, expertise, communication, and learning.
runbook.advanceWhen: Most students have chosen two and you have heard several explanations.
runbook.openWith: This is your career question, not just today's class question.
runbook.whyMatters: Turns the activity into a forward-looking skills decision.
runbook.ask: What capability helps a human use AI well across many different tools?
runbook.pause: Vote, reveal, then discuss the top 2–3.
runbook.listenFor: Judgment, expertise, adaptability, communication, problem framing.
runbook.ifTheySay: Prompt engineering → ask whether that remains rare once tools improve and everyone learns it.
runbook.ifQuiet: Ask which skill a manager notices when the AI output is wrong.
runbook.pushFurther: Which skill are you currently building evidence of—not merely claiming on a résumé?
runbook.sayDuringReveal: The interesting part is the combination: AI capability plus distinctly human judgment and expertise.
runbook.landHere: AI literacy becomes more valuable when it is paired with judgment, domain knowledge, communication, and the ability to learn.
runbook.transition: Finish by applying this to yourself.
runbook.sourceNotes: LinkedIn Labor Market Report 2026 reports U.S. jobs requiring AI-literacy skills grew 70% year over year. WEF Sept. 2026 reports employers increasingly value learning agility, emotional intelligence, and other human capabilities alongside AI skills.

steps.label: 🏁 EXIT TICKET
steps.title: What will YOU do differently because AI is changing work?
steps.lead: Finish the three sentences. Your reasoning is the final submission.
steps.studentTask: Submit: 1) AI will probably change my future work by ____. 2) One skill I need to strengthen is ____. 3) One workplace decision I would not allow AI to make alone is ____ because ____.
steps.visualCaption: What will you delegate? What will you verify? What will you own?

runbook.say: Don't give me 'AI will change everything.' Make this specific to your future work and your responsibility as the human.
runbook.askNext: What will you delegate, what will you verify, and what will you still own?
runbook.watchFor: Generic statements. Encourage students to name a task, a skill, and a decision with a reason.
runbook.advanceWhen: Most students have submitted or the 75-minute mark arrives.
runbook.openWith: Last five minutes—back to individual thinking.
runbook.whyMatters: Captures individual evidence of transfer from the team exercise to each student's future work.
runbook.ask: What is one boundary you can defend?
runbook.landHere: Your competitive advantage is not simply having AI. It is knowing what to delegate, how to evaluate what comes back, and when the human must take control.
runbook.transition: Save your thinking. This is a career skill, not just an AI-literacy concept.
